newsitem.title: USA: New AIDS drugs available for children, adults.
newsitem.headline: New AIDS drugs available for children, adults.

text.p: Two AIDS drugs were approved for use by children on Friday, the first specific protease inhibitors for pediatric AIDS in the United States, federal health officials said.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said it had approved Agouron Pharmaceutical's nelfinavir, to be sold under the brand name Viracept, the fourth protease inhibitor on the market. It was approved for both adults and children.
The FDA also gave Abbott Laboratories' ritonavir, sold under the brand name Norvir, approval for pediatric use. It has been available to adults for about a year.

Protease inhibitors, used in combination with older anti-viral drugs, have transformed AIDS treatment. Though not a cure, these combination therapies have suppressed the virus to undetectable levels in many patients and prolonged their lives.

Once a drug is approved for adults, doctors can use it legally for children but formal FDA approval generally increases pediatric use and gives doctors more specific information about dosages for children.

The FDA has simplified the process for getting pediatric use information on the label, particularly in serious or life-threatening illnesses. Such information can now be provided when the course of the disease or the effect of the drug are sufficiently similar in children and adults.
Agouron said Viracept will be widely available at U.S. pharmacies next week.

The wholesale price of Viracept will be $15.48 per day or $5,650 for a 365-day supply at the recommended dose of 750 mg three times daily. Agouron has established a patient assistance programme to help people who cannot pay for the drug.
